$comment: AUTHORED — the one file you edit to add or change a map layer. Run `pnpm style:build`, then commit the generated style.json + style.meta.json. Colours reference tokens; the VALUES that drive a colouring are not in the tiles, so every non-static mode must name the provider it reads. Source layer names and featureIdProperty must match pipeline/deliver/tiles/layers.py exactly — they did not, and a mismatch draws nothing while erroring nowhere.

atlas.$comment: our pipeline's tiles: geometry, identity and administrative geography. No regulation data — see pipeline/deliver/tiles/layers.py.

imagery.attribution: Powered by Esri · Source: Esri, Vantor, Earthstar Geographics, and the GIS User Community
imagery.$comment: SATELLITE IMAGERY — Esri World Imagery, ONLINE-ONLY (owner 2026-10-21, handoff/PLAN/app-integration/decisions.md; research and terms: handoff/PLAN/app-data/satellite/README.md). The URL is Esri's own ArcGIS Online World_Imagery MapServer tile endpoint, as the original app used it (2026-03); a build with an ArcGIS Location Platform key swaps it whole at run time (`imageryTiles`, EXPO_PUBLIC_ARCGIS_API_KEY) — never a key in this file. `blankTile=false`: where Esri has no imagery at a zoom (rural BC stops at z17-18) it answers 404 instead of a grey 'Map data not yet available' tile, and the renderer overzooms the parent. maxzoom 19 is Esri's (urban BC goes deeper); its tiles are 256 px, so the z18 camera asks for z19 tiles, and rural holes 404 to the parent. Never stored or packaged: Esri's item terms say the layer is 'not intended to be used to export tiles for offline'. The attribution is Esri's required form ('Powered by Esri' + the service's copyrightText, read 2026-10-21) and rides on the source so MapLibre's control shows it exactly while the layer is drawn; @app/core IMAGERY_CREDIT holds the same words for the app's credit list (tools/imagery.test.ts). Tiles send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, which WebGL needs.

basins.$comment: THE SAME ARCHIVE AS `atlas`, read as a second source that STOPS at z7 — the last zoom the tile builder writes basin polygons at (`basin` maxzoom = BASIN_HANDOVER_Z - 1 in pipeline/deliver/tiles/layers.py). MapLibre overzooms a source past its maxzoom, so the z7 tiles carry the field across [7, 8) up to the handover (z8 since T130, owner 2026-10-22: "should be able to zoom out quite a bit more first"; it was z10). An archive built while the handover was z9 also holds z8 basin tiles; they are never asked for. On `atlas` itself the field could never outlive the tiles: at z9 MapLibre asks the archive for z9 tiles, which carry no basins, and the field vanished a zoom before the rivers came back. Only the basin layer reads it, and that layer is drawn only while the field is on (`field.drawnIn`), so the Map tab never fetches through it.

mus.$comment: THE SAME ARCHIVE AS `atlas`, read as a source that STOPS at z12 for the management units (T202, owner 2026-10-27). The tile builder writes `mu` only to z12, in its own pass with z12 as that pass's top zoom (pipeline/deliver/tiles/tippe.py `MU_MAX_ZOOM`), so z12 keeps a finer edge (~8 m at most on the ground) and MapLibre overzooms it from z13 to the camera's z18. On `atlas` the units would vanish at z13, where the archive has none. Saves ~7 MB: in the atlas every z13 tile also holds streams, so mu's squares never deduped there. TO REVERSE: set `MU_MAX_ZOOM` back to the archive's max zoom in tippe.py, point the `mu` layer back at `atlas` and drop this source.

groups.label: Parks and reserves
groups.$comment: Off by default. Parks and ecological reserves are large opaque areas and they buried the water they sit around — the map's job is to say which water is open, and an overlay that hides the water fails at it. Behind Layers.

groups.label: Land access
groups.$comment: Off by default, for the same reason as `protected`: these are big fills, and the answer is the water. A user who needs to know where they may not go turns it on, and then it is the point of the screen rather than noise on it.

groups.label: Satellite imagery
groups.$comment: NOT a group a screen toggles. Imagery replaces the drawn ground, so it is switched as the map's `basemap` prop (adapter `setBasemap`), never through `groups` — which is how a screen could otherwise light it while the drawn basemap and its wash still competed underneath.

groups.label: Fish obstacles
groups.$comment: (T173) Falls, cascades, canyons, velocity barriers, culverts and dams (pipeline/deliver/tiles/obstacles.py: FISS + WRIS, Open Government Licence – BC). A switch in the Layers sheet (`overlay.obstacles`), off by default: context about the water, never part of its answer.

layers.$comment: The satellite ground. Drawn UNDER everything of ours and under the outside-BC mask — the runtime places raster layers directly over the drawn basemap's ground, so the mask still says where we have no answers. No colour modes: a photograph has no colouring to choose, and the builder exempts raster layers from that rule for exactly this reason.

A WATERSHED A REGULATION NAMES (today only the Liard, 142,173 km2; owner 2026-10-27, T202): a darker green wash UNDER every other layer, so a reader sees where the watershed rule applies without a border competing with the water. No outline: a drainage divide is not a line anyone fishes across, and the ground is what changes. The tile carries geometry only (decorative: the area's id and name live in the bundle's `area:` items), so nothing here is tapped or labelled.

QUIET ON PURPOSE (owner 2026-10-22: "private land is very abrasive when turned on" and "should show slightly more zoomed out"). A warm tint at `opacity.parcel` and a hairline edge at `opacity.parcel.edge`, under every water colour (first of our layers). From z11: the tile builder now writes the parcel layer from z11 too (pipeline/deliver/tiles/layers.py `parcel` minzoom; about +2 MB of tiles, measured). The atlas shipped today was built at z12, so until the next atlas build z11 asks for parcels the tiles do not have and the layer still starts at z12.

Reserves and treaty lands, in v1's dark goldenrod. AN ACCESS ADVISORY, NEVER A FISHING CLOSURE — which is why it is brown and not hatched: the crimson-and-hatch language on this map means the water is closed, and saying that here would be both wrong and offensive. Brown is the OSM convention for it and carries no restriction meaning.

outline.$comment: v1's ADMIN_BORDER_MINZOOM. The hatch and the tint carry this area at a distance; the border is for when you are close enough to want to know exactly where it runs. Drawn from z4 it is one more line in a province already full of them.

CRISP CLOSE IN (owner 2026-10-22: restricted and closed areas nicer at every zoom). From z10 a solid edge in the area's own status colour, a hairline at first and firm by street scale — where the hatch alone made the boundary a guess at the edge of a weave. Below z10 there is no edge at all: the hatch carries the area.

CRISP CLOSE IN (owner 2026-10-22: restricted and closed areas nicer at every zoom). From z10 a solid edge in the area's own status colour, a hairline at first and firm by street scale — where the hatch alone made the boundary a guess at the edge of a weave. Below z10 there is no edge at all: the hatch carries the area.

layers.$comment: LAND YOU MAY ENTER, WITH PERMISSION — the UBC Malcolm Knapp Research Forest and three others. AMBER, NOT CRIMSON, and hatched like a closure because it is one until you have asked. v1 used the same two-tier red/amber language. These four were dropped from the map entirely until the `permit_land_access` area def existed.
Its own layer, not a park variant: it is a blanket closure and must never be styled like somewhere you may fish.

outline.$comment: CRISP CLOSE IN (owner 2026-10-22: restricted and closed areas nicer at every zoom). From z10 a solid edge in the area's own status colour, a hairline at first and firm by street scale — where the hatch alone made the boundary a guess at the edge of a weave. Below z10 there is no edge at all: the hatch carries the area.

layers.$comment: PROVINCIAL PARKS AND PROTECTED AREAS — open water, in v1's green. NO OUTLINE, deliberately: a border is an assertion that the line matters, and here it does not. You may fish on both sides of it. Every bordered area on this map is one where crossing the line changes what you may do, and provincial parks would have been the only exception, which is exactly how a reader learns to stop trusting borders.

outline.$comment: CRISP CLOSE IN (owner 2026-10-22: restricted and closed areas nicer at every zoom). From z10 a solid edge in the area's own status colour, a hairline at first and firm by street scale — where the hatch alone made the boundary a guess at the edge of a weave. Below z10 there is no edge at all: the hatch carries the area.

layers.$comment: NATIONAL PARKS AND THE CHILKOOT TRAIL — federal closures, drawn in v1's crimson and HATCHED. The hatch is the message: on a paper chart diagonal lines mean keep out, and a flat red tint would read as merely another kind of area. `kind` is what separates these from provincial parks in the same tile layer — a park with a kind of its own is a park with its own closing authority.

(T166, owner 2026-10-28) TIDAL WATER: the DFO tidal-waters polygon (all BC coastal sea and the estuaries) plus the footprints of the stream pieces removed below a tidal boundary (pipeline/deliver/tiles). Freshwater regulations stop here; DFO's tidal rules begin. Drawn UNDER every freshwater layer (first in the water group, before the basin field) as a muted sea-teal wash and a thin edge, STATIC in every colour mode. NOT decorative: it carries `area_id` (always "tidal") and `name` ("Tidal water"), property-based identity and no MVT id, so it is a tap target of its own — asked after the obstacle mark and the water sections (src/sections.ts `TIDAL_LAYERS`), opening the tidal sheet (`@app/core` `tidalSheet`). The tile has minzoom 6, maxzoom 13 (overzoomed past it). The label is the tile `name`; the full wording lives in the sheet.

standing.label: Flow for the date
standing.$comment:
THE SAME STOPS AS THE RIVERS, from the same place, because it is the same question asked of a bigger shape. A second ramp here would be a second legend for one scale.

WITHOUT THE -1 SENTINEL, which the rivers keep. On a reach, "a gauge reports here but has no record to rank it against" is worth drawing: you can tap it and be told. On a 3,600 km2 region it is a purple blotch the size of a valley that a reader cannot interrogate, and at this zoom the map should be answering one question in one vocabulary. Such a group falls through to `missing` — the unmeasured grey — which is the same thing the map says about a group with no gauge at all, and at this scale that is the truthful pairing.

`missing` is water.ungauged: the grey a river gets when nothing can speak for it.

layers.$comment:
THE PROVINCE AS A FIELD, below the zoom where a river is a hairline.

A percentile is a claim about a CATCHMENT, which is why the discs this replaces were wrong: a disc paints land the gauge says nothing about, two overlapping discs blend into a colour that is not on the scale, and a blurred edge is a lighter shade — on a sequential ramp, a different number. These are the Province's own named watersheds and they have edges.

THIS LAYER'S `maxzoom` IS THE HANDOVER — the one number (T130): emitted as `field.handover`, read by the app as `FIELD_HANDOVER_Z` (camera bit, taps: `tapOpensWater`), and every layer in `field.covers` stands down below it. z8 since T130 (owner 2026-10-22: "should be able to zoom out quite a bit more first"; it was z10): measured at z6-z10, the coloured rivers read at z8 and break into hairline fragments at z7. `BASIN_HANDOVER_Z` in the tile builder is held to the same number (tools/handover.test.ts).

MAXZOOM IS EXCLUSIVE, and this was written as if it were inclusive. MapLibre hides a layer at zoom >= maxzoom, so `maxzoom: 8` meant the field stopped at 8.0 while the rivers, standing down below 9, did not start until 9.0 — a full zoom level, and a common resting place, drawing NEITHER. Zooming out of Conditions showed the rivers vanish and the province stay blank until the next step. It is the handover zoom itself: the field draws below the handover, the rivers from it, and the two meet exactly. The TILE stops one zoom short (z7 since T130) — the last basin tile overzooms across the final step — which is why the builder's basin maxzoom and this one differ by one (tools/handover.test.ts).

field.$comment:
ONE ANSWER PER ZOOM, AND NOTHING UNDER IT (owner 2026-10-22: "the lakes and streams etc disappear when it is visible"). While the field is drawn (`drawnIn`: its colour modes that draw at all — `plain` is not drawn, it was a #D5D5D5 wash at 0.55 over the whole Map tab below z9), every layer in `covers` takes the field's maxzoom as its floor: the rivers and lakes and their names, outlines, arrows and dashes, the wetlands, the routes through lakes, and the basemap's own river lines (`runtime`: layers the style does not generate, with the floor each returns to). Under the field before, the lake outlines, the lake names from z8 and the no-baseline dashes all drew through it — two answers, one of them a hairline. Released the moment the field is: the Map tab and the temperature view keep every layer's own floor.

ONE SOLID SHEET (review 2026-10-22). The tile build simplifies each basin on its own, so neighbours do not share an edge: 3,552 slivers open between them and 3,694 overlap, up to ~700 m across. Drawn translucent and overzoomed from z8 to z10 those were white and black wedges a valley long, every overlap a darker seam, and the basemap's lakes and the Fraser showed through. So the field is OPAQUE, each colour pre-mixed on `over` at the layer's own opacity token (the colour the 0.55 field had on blank paper, now without the ground showing through), and the seam under it (`outline`, `under`) closes the gaps. Nothing under the field can show through it; `covers` still stands those layers down so their names and the gauge dots, which draw above every fill, do not float over it. The source fix (basins simplified as one coverage, pipeline/deliver/tiles/basins.py) lands with the next atlas build; the seam keeps the field closed until then.

outline.$comment: THE SEAM, under the field in each basin's own colour: it shows only where no basin is drawn, so it closes the slivers between independently simplified neighbours without moving a border. Wide enough for the widest (~700 m) at every zoom the field draws: 700 m is 1.7 px at z8, the handover, at 49 N; the curve ends there with the field (tools/handover.test.ts holds it to the gap below the handover).

layers.$comment: Marsh and swamp — the largest layer by area in the province, and CONTEXT rather than an answer. It is HATCHED (see src/hatch.ts): texture is what lets it read at 45% where a flat wash needs 60% and buries every river it surrounds. The pattern applies to the static colouring ONLY: a fill that carries a data-driven answer must win over the weave. `filter`: only polygons whose `water` (the registry's kind) is not `stream` — a slough drawn as a wetland is `wetland_flowing`'s.

standing.label: Flow for the date
standing.$comment:
The PERCENTILE for this day of year, not the discharge: 15.7 m3/s is a flood on one creek and a drought on another.  STOPS SIT AT THE PERCENTILES THEY NAME. Even sixths gave half the ramp to the outer tenths, where almost nothing ever sits, and squeezed 'normal' — the middle half of the record — into one step. Now 25..75 is half the scale, which is what it is.  EVERY STOP IS MID-DARK. The ramp used to pass through a sandy beige a shade off the basemap's own paper, so the middle of the scale vanished over land; a ramp for a map may not contain the ground's colour.  `missing` is water.ungauged, a faint grey: most reaches have no gauge entitled to speak for them, and that is not the same as a rule we could not parse, nor the same claim as water.unmapped, which is about the atlas rather than about measurement.

THE -1 SENTINEL IS NO LONGER A COLOUR. "Measured here, but nothing to compare it to" was a purple on a sequential ramp — where every other colour means a position between low and high, and that one means the axis does not exist here. It is now the same neutral grey as water nothing speaks for, and the difference is carried by a DASH: `stream-nobaseline` in runtime-style.ts, its own layer because `line-dasharray` cannot be varied per feature. A dash reads as provisional without competing for a place on the scale, and it survives a colour-blind palette.

profile.label: Status for the date
profile.$comment: THE DAY'S STATUS, the fast way (colour-latency study, AP). Feature-state `p` holds the section's PROFILE label (`profileLabel` in @app/core: `p<n>`, or `b` for a section the index does not list), set by the renderer once per section per session as each tile arrives; the DAY lives in the paint as one match over the labels (`dayProfiles` in @app/core, beside `statusOfCode`), so a day change is one paint property and no per-section call. Same three tokens as `status`, so a search row's dot and this line cannot disagree. `missing` is a label in no set — no profile pushed yet, or tidal / outside B.C. — and wears the neutral `water.unmapped` grey, never base. With no day installed (no proven pair, or the index withdrawn) the adapter paints the layer's plain mode instead: not asked is never drawn as an answer.

salmon.label: Salmon for the date
salmon.$comment: (T211) THE SALMON COLOURING, the fast way — the `profile` mode's engine, its own channel: feature-state `sp` holds the section's DFO CHAIN label (`s<chain>`, @app/core `salmonLabel`, fixed for the release), set as each tile arrives; the DAY lives in the paint as one match over the chain labels (`salmonDayProfiles`). Toggling Standard / Salmon is one paint change per layer: no fetch, no relabel. A section DFO does not list reads the UNLISTED chain (closed to salmon fishing, owner 2026-10-27) — an answer, not `missing`; `missing` is only a section not labelled yet. Its own tokens (`salmon.*`), never the provincial `status.*`, so the two colourings read apart.

layers.$comment: The same for a slough drawn as a WETLAND polygon (Taylor Slough): stream colours, no hatch — the weave says 'marsh' and this is not one. See `lake_flowing`.

standing.label: Flow for the date
standing.$comment:
THE SAME SCALE AS THE RIVERS, from the same stops, because it is the same question and a lake coloured on a scale of its own would be a second legend nobody asked for.

A lake gets a reading only where a station sits IN it — `lake_gauge`, 196 rows — and there is no prediction for the rest. Nothing in this app can carry a level from one lake to another: a lake's stage is set by its outlet and its own storage, not by how wet the country is, so an ungauged lake stays at `water.ungauged` exactly as an ungauged river does. The grey is the honest answer, not a gap in the data.

THE -1 SENTINEL IS NO LONGER A COLOUR. "Measured here, but nothing to compare it to" was a purple on a sequential ramp — where every other colour means a position between low and high, and that one means the axis does not exist here. It is now the same neutral grey as water nothing speaks for, and the difference is carried by a DASH: `stream-nobaseline` in runtime-style.ts, its own layer because `line-dasharray` cannot be varied per feature. A dash reads as provisional without competing for a place on the scale, and it survives a colour-blind palette.

surveyed.label: Depth
surveyed.$comment: Depth is about which lakes have been SURVEYED, not only which have digitised contours. 2,741 bathymetric sheets exist and only a fraction were ever traced into vector contours — colouring by contours alone shows a near-empty map and tells a reader the province was never surveyed, which is the opposite of true.

outline.$comment:
Same colour as the streams, as v1 had it: a lake and the river through it are one water, and an outline in a different hue reads as a different thing. Width scales with the SQUARE ROOT of area — area grows as the square of a shoreline, so a linear ramp makes Babine enormous and every small lake invisible.

FOLLOWS THE FILL wherever the fill is answering a question. A lake filled by its flow percentile and ringed in plain blue was drawing two answers at once — the edge said 'water' while the middle said 'much below normal', and the edge is the part that survives at a distance where the fill is a few pixels. `plain` is excluded: there the fill IS the water colour, so an inherited edge would disappear into it.
outline.$comment_drawAfter: A WATER LINE, NOT A FILL (T83). The shoreline wears the lake's status colour, so it is drawn with the streams, after the region and unit boundaries; the fill stays here, under them. Where a boundary crosses a lake it runs over the fill (traceable) and under the shoreline (the water's answer wins).

label.$comment: BIG LAKES GET NAMED EARLIER, and win collisions when they compete. `showAbove` is v1's area ladder — 5 km2 at z8, 1 km2 at z9, 0.1 km2 at z10, everything from z11 — and `sortBy: area_m2` becomes a NEGATED symbol-sort-key, so a cluster of ponds can no longer crowd out the lake somebody actually came looking for. Both read the same `area_m2` the outline width does, which is why that attribute survives.

layers.$comment: A STREAM'S POLYGON — a river's wide reach, a slough, a canal (the Vedder Canal, the Stellako's) — drawn from the `lake` source-layer but in STREAM colours, in every mode (user ruling 2026-10-03: a slough is a stream everywhere, and must look like one). The tile's `water` property is the registry's water kind, the same `item.kind` the bundle carries, so the map and the sheet cannot disagree about what the water is; `lake` draws the rest (its inverse filter). No label and no outline: the river's own route is written into the `stream` layer under this polygon's section id (pipeline tiles/export.py), which carries the name along the line and fills the hole at the zooms the polygon is not yet drawn at. Status is pushed on the `lake` source-layer (`statusData`), and feature-state is per source-layer, so this layer sees it. Not in `highlight`'s own id space: `selected` on `lake` already lights it.

NOT FISHING WATER (T152, Q125 owner 2026-10-24): sewage settling basins, mine tailing ponds and dumps. They hold water and no rule speaks of them, so they are drawn as a MUTED FILL in a ground colour — never in a water colour, never as a lake: a lake-blue polygon reads as water you may fish under the region's rules. NO featureIdProperty and not highlightable, deliberately, as `under_lake`: the tile layer is `decorative` (pipeline layers.py — no attributes, no id), so it is in no tap group (src/sections.ts `TAP_GROUPS`) and a tap on one resolves to nothing. Static in every view; covered by the Conditions field like the other water fills.

width.$comment: v1's exact curve, and NO ATTRIBUTE. A route through a lake is a construction line: it says the river continues, not how big it is. Drawn at the mainstem's own Strahler weight — which it briefly was — it stops reading as a note and starts reading as more river, which is the one confusion this layer exists to avoid. The lake's own outline already carries the size.

layers.$comment:
The route a river takes THROUGH a lake — connectivity, not water you can fish. A lake with several inflows has a route from each, so at full weight the layer reads as a spider web over every lake in the province. It has to be the thinnest, faintest thing on the map: a dotted hairline that says 'the river continues' and nothing more.

IT HAS NO featureIdProperty, deliberately. It is decoration: a person tapping the dotted thread means the LAKE, so the route is out of the tap query, out of `highlightable`, and its tile carries no attributes at all (pipeline layers.py marks it `decorative`). Promoting an id it does not ship would leave every feature with id `undefined` and a tap resolving to nothing.

label.$comment:
The big number in the middle, z4 to z7 — and then it stops, because from z7 the unit boundaries appear and their numbers take over. Two administrative numbering systems on screen at once is how a reader ends up fishing under the wrong table.

MEDIUM, NOT BOLD. The glyph host does not serve a 'Noto Sans Bold' face — every range 404s — so this label asked for a font that does not exist and rendered nothing at all. There is no error a reader can see: MapLibre requests the range, gets a 404, and draws no text. `tools/check-style.mjs` now holds the font list to the faces the host actually has.

layers.$comment: SOLID AND HEAVIER THAN A UNIT. The regulations are organised by region, so this is the boundary that changes which table you are reading; the unit boundary inside it only refines it. v1 drew regions solid at 2-4.5 px and units dotted at 1.2-1.8, and that weight difference is the whole hierarchy.

OVER THE WATER'S FILLS, UNDER ITS LINES (T83). Source order is draw order, and `mu` used to be first of ten — so its boundary was painted under every lake fill, every wetland hatch and every river on the map. An administrative line the ground is drawn on top of is not a line anybody can follow; v1 put the region and unit boundaries above the water for that reason. But last of all put them over every status line too: a grey dotted unit line cut a closed river into pieces and the boundary, which only says where a table changes, won over the colour that is the answer. So both boundaries sit between the fills and the water lines — after `under_lake`, before `stream`, and the lake's shoreline (`lake.outline.drawAfter`) is held back until after this layer. tools/layer-order.test.ts holds it.

The fill is near-invisible (`opacity.admin.fill`); it exists so the shape can be tapped and so a label has an anchor, not to be looked at.

outline.$comment: DOTTED, as v1 drew it, and from z7 only. A unit boundary is an administrative line over country, not a feature of the country; solid it competes with every river it crosses. Below z7 there are 225 of them on one screen and `region` is drawn instead.

label.$comment:
INSIDE THE UNIT, NOT ALONG ITS EDGE.
This was `placement: line` on a POLYGON, which puts the number on the boundary itself, repeated every 200px. Two units share that boundary, so both numbers landed on the same line and neither said which side it belonged to — the one question a reader has at a boundary is 'which unit am I standing in', and a number sitting on the fence answers it for neither side.
Point placement on a polygon anchors the label at the shape's interior, so 4-18 reads inside 4-18. MapLibre places one symbol per polygon PER TILE, and a unit spans many tiles at z8+, so the number follows you around inside the unit instead of appearing once at a centroid you may never have on screen.
`region` one layer up has always done this; the unit label was the odd one out.

layers.$comment: A CLOSURE BOUNDED BY SIGNS (Fraser at Landstrom Bar, Skeena at the Kispiox confluence; hand-drawn rings in data/curated/waters/added_areas.geojson): a DASHED edge in the closed colour and a slight tint inside (owner 2026-10-27, T202). Dashed because the line on the ground is a pair of signs, not a surveyed boundary. Over the water's fills and under its lines, like `mu`, so the river's own status colour still answers on top. Not tapped, like every other area: a tap means the river, which is already cut at the ring and carries the closure itself.

width.$comment: v1's formula, from archive/webapp/src/map/styles.ts. Width is LINEAR in Strahler order — base + order x slope — and both move with zoom. The shape is the point: at z4 order barely matters (0.1 per order), so a zoomed-out province reads as a uniform hairline network; by z14 order dominates (1.5 per order) and the Fraser is obviously the Fraser. Two attempts at a piecewise ramp over order got the magnitudes into range and the SHAPE wrong — everything was differentiated at every zoom, so the low-zoom map was a mess of competing weights.

standing.label: Flow for the date
standing.$comment:
The PERCENTILE for this day of year, not the discharge: 15.7 m3/s is a flood on one creek and a drought on another.  STOPS SIT AT THE PERCENTILES THEY NAME. Even sixths gave half the ramp to the outer tenths, where almost nothing ever sits, and squeezed 'normal' — the middle half of the record — into one step. Now 25..75 is half the scale, which is what it is.  EVERY STOP IS MID-DARK. The ramp used to pass through a sandy beige a shade off the basemap's own paper, so the middle of the scale vanished over land; a ramp for a map may not contain the ground's colour.  `missing` is water.ungauged, a faint grey: most reaches have no gauge entitled to speak for them, and that is not the same as a rule we could not parse, nor the same claim as water.unmapped, which is about the atlas rather than about measurement.

THE -1 SENTINEL IS NO LONGER A COLOUR. "Measured here, but nothing to compare it to" was a purple on a sequential ramp — where every other colour means a position between low and high, and that one means the axis does not exist here. It is now the same neutral grey as water nothing speaks for, and the difference is carried by a DASH: `stream-nobaseline` in runtime-style.ts, its own layer because `line-dasharray` cannot be varied per feature. A dash reads as provisional without competing for a place on the scale, and it survives a colour-blind palette.

profile.label: Status for the date
profile.$comment: THE DAY'S STATUS, the fast way (colour-latency study, AP). Feature-state `p` holds the section's PROFILE label (`profileLabel` in @app/core: `p<n>`, or `b` for a section the index does not list), set by the renderer once per section per session as each tile arrives; the DAY lives in the paint as one match over the labels (`dayProfiles` in @app/core, beside `statusOfCode`), so a day change is one paint property and no per-section call. Same three tokens as `status`, so a search row's dot and this line cannot disagree. `missing` is a label in no set — no profile pushed yet, or tidal / outside B.C. — and wears the neutral `water.unmapped` grey, never base. With no day installed (no proven pair, or the index withdrawn) the adapter paints the layer's plain mode instead: not asked is never drawn as an answer.

salmon.label: Salmon for the date
salmon.$comment: (T211) THE SALMON COLOURING, the fast way — the `profile` mode's engine, its own channel: feature-state `sp` holds the section's DFO CHAIN label (`s<chain>`, @app/core `salmonLabel`, fixed for the release), set as each tile arrives; the DAY lives in the paint as one match over the chain labels (`salmonDayProfiles`). Toggling Standard / Salmon is one paint change per layer: no fetch, no relabel. A section DFO does not list reads the UNLISTED chain (closed to salmon fishing, owner 2026-10-27) — an answer, not `missing`; `missing` is only a section not labelled yet. Its own tokens (`salmon.*`), never the provincial `status.*`, so the two colourings read apart.

label.$comment: v1's stream labels, restored. `symbol-placement: line` is the whole character of a river map: the name bends along the water the way it does on a paper chart, and a point label on a 200 km line would sit at one arbitrary vertex. Nothing below z11 — at z10 the province is a network, not a set of named rivers, and every label would be a collision.

arrows.$comment: WHICH WAY THE WATER GOES, on the Conditions map (owner 2026-10-21). A glyph laid along the line and CHOSEN to point DOWNSTREAM by the tile contract's `flows` (stream lines run mouth to source, measured on the live atlas), in the stream's own colour with a paper halo, drawn only where a view shows it (`views[].show`: Conditions). From z9, where the Conditions rivers come back after the basin field; big water first (Strahler order 6+ at z9, everything from z13) so a valley is not a field of chevrons, and placed after every name so a name never loses its spot to an arrow. A glyph, not an `addImage` icon: the phone has no runtime-image API (N2-F1) and the fonts ship with every release.

layers.$comment: (T173) The paper ring under each obstacle mark (MapLibre circles are drawn here without a stroke): it lifts the ink dot off a status-coloured stream line, which is where nearly every mark sits.

(T173) FISH OBSTACLES, as small marks: an ink dot in a paper ring, one look for every type (the tap sheet says which). SMALL AND COLOURLESS ON PURPOSE: the colours on this map are answers (a status, a gauge's reading), and a mark that wore one would read as one. Distinct from a gauge (a coloured dot, the Conditions map's) and a spot (a pin). Tapped before the water under it (`sections.ts` OBSTACLE_LAYERS, `MapProps.onPressObstacle`). From z10, the tile layer's own minzoom.

views.label: Conditions
views.$comment: HIDE, NOT A GROUP TOGGLE. Management-unit and region boundaries answer "which table of regulations governs here", which is not a question the Conditions map is asking — over a flow field they are lines a reader has to learn to ignore. The app tried to turn them off by passing `admin: false` in `groups`, and the `admin` group is deliberately NOT toggleable, so the adapter refused it: the boundaries kept drawing and the console filled with "layer group admin is not toggleable". Which layers a VIEW draws is a property of the view, so it is stated here rather than asserted by a screen.

views.label: Water temperature
views.$comment: THE WATER IS DRAWN PLAIN AND THE ANSWER IS ON THE DOTS. Every other view colours the river, because a flow percentile can be carried from a gauge to the water around it. Temperature cannot yet — that needs the donor panel — and colouring a river from a station 40 km away would be inventing a number for water nobody measured. So the stations say what they read and the rivers say nothing, which is the truth today.\n\nIt is also a different SET of stations: 274 of the 439 publish a temperature against 361 that publish a discharge, and they are not the same 274.

views.label: Plain map
views.$comment: THE DEFAULT, because regulations are not integrated. The Map tab draws water in its neutral colour; the per-layer modes the app sets (stocked, surveyed, standing) are applied over this. The `regulations` view and the `closure` colour mode it used were removed with the regulation integration — see app/packages/core/src/regulations.ts.

providers.$comment: Where a colour mode's values come from. Tiles carry IDENTITY (section_id) and almost nothing else — discharge, stocking and survey facts live in the bundle and the live feeds. The app fetches per visible feature and pushes feature-state; the tiles never change.

gauges.$comment: 450 stations, 30-min refresh. Keyed by SECTION, bridged to a station by the build's `section_gauge` precompute — and only where the magnitude ratio says that station can speak for the reach. Below the floor the section has no link at all and reports no gauge rather than borrowing a big river's number. It was declared `item_id`/`item_to_sections`, which is how stocking works, not this.

stocking.$comment: per-waterbody release records, refreshed weekly. Two weeks is the stale threshold: one missed run is normal, two means the job is broken. Bound to item_id — stocking is INTO a lake, not onto a reach.

lakes.$comment: Per-lake facts from the bundle: whether the lake was surveyed, and when it was last stocked. Keyed by section because that is what the tile carries; the fanout resolves it to the item the fact belongs to.

status.$comment: THE STATUS INDEX (`status_index.bin`, `python -m pipeline.deliver.status_index`): closed / own / base for every section on any day, precomputed from the bundle through the reference reader and pinned to the same section_handles digest as the tiles. Keyed by the tile's own section_id, so colouring needs no bundle query. A section the file does not list is BASE — absence is a claim the pipeline made, so `missing` paints base; the app only selects this mode once the index has loaded and matched the tiles' vintage.

salmon.$comment: (T211) THE DFO SALMON (`salmon/1`, pipeline/deliver/salmon.py): each section's chain of DFO locations and each chain's map status per day, precomputed at deliver time and pinned to the same section_handles digest as the tiles. A section the file does not place is the unlisted chain: closed to salmon fishing.

method.$comment: (T213) BAIT BAN AND FLY FISHING ONLY (`method/1`, pipeline/deliver/method.py): each section's day-profile of none / bait ban / fly only, projected at deliver time from the answers' open-days strips and pinned to the same section_handles digest as the tiles. A section the file does not list is none every day; closures are the status index's.

$toggleable_groups:
WHAT MAY BE SWITCHED OFF, and what may not.

`protected` and `access` are NOT toggleable and are ON by default. A national park, an ecological reserve, an Indian reserve and land the public may not enter are all reasons a person can be somewhere they should not be, and none of them is a preference. They were both toggleable and hidden by default, which meant the map's normal state was one that showed none of them.

`ownership` IS toggleable and off by default, and that asymmetry is the point: title is context, not an instruction. It carries private land ONLY — most of British Columbia is Crown land, so drawing that would be a wash over the whole province saying almost nothing. Private title on the bank you meant to walk down is worth looking up deliberately.
$comment_order: DRAW ORDER IS SOURCE ORDER. Areas, then the water's fills, then the administrative boundaries, then the water's LINES (the lake shoreline via `outline.drawAfter`, then the streams), and labels last (the generator appends those itself). A boundary painted under a lake is a boundary nobody can trace; a boundary painted over a status line hides the answer (T83, tools/layer-order.test.ts).
